subtopic: Continuous Random Variables and Probability Density Function
stem:
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is \(f(x) = 3x^2\), for \(0 < x < 1\). Note that \(f(x)\) is not \(P[X = x]\).
For example, \(f(0.9) = 3(0.9)^2 = 2.43 > 1\), which is clearly not a probability. In the continuous case, \(f(x)\) is the height of the curve at \(X = x\), so that the total area under the curve is 1. Here it is areas under the curve that define the probabilities.
Verify that \(f(x)\) is a proper probability density function. Also, for real numbers \(c\) and \(d\) such that \(0 \leq c < d \leq 1\), find \(P[c < X < d]\). Hence answer the following.
(a) What is the probability that \(X\) falls between \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) and 1? That is, what is \(P\left[\dfrac{1}{2} < X < 1\right]\)?
(b) What is \(P\left(X = \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\)?
solution:
Now, let's start by verifying that \(f(x)\) is a valid probability density function.
For this, note the following results.
1. \(f(x) = 3x^2 \geq 0\) for all \(x \in [0, 1]\).
2. \(\int_{0}^{1} f(x) = \int_{0}^{1} 3x^2\, dx = 1\)
Therefore, the function \(f(x) = 3x^2\), for \(0 < x < 1\) is a proper probability density function.
Also, for real numbers \(c\) and \(d\) such that \(0 \leq c < d \leq 1\), note that
\(P[c < X < d] = \int_{c}^{d} f(x)\, dx = \int_{c}^{d} 3x^2\, dx = \left[x^3\right]_{c}^{d} = d^3 - c^3 > 0\)
(a) Substitute \(c = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(d = 1\) in the above integral to obtain
\(P\left[\dfrac{1}{2} < X < 1\right] = 1^3 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 1 - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{7}{8}\).
(b) See that the probability is 0. This is so because
\(\int_{c}^{d} f(x)\, dx = \int_{1/2}^{1/2} x^3\, dx = 1 - 1 = 0\).
[The ordinate AB, with \(A\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\, 0\right)\) and \(B\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\, \dfrac{1}{8}\right)\) is degenerate case of rectangle and has area 0]
As a matter of fact, in general, if \(X\) is a continuous random variable, then the probability that \(X\) takes any specific value \(x\) is 0. That is, when \(X\) is a continuous random variable, then
\(P[X = x] = 0\) for every \(x\) in the support.

subtopic: Continuous Random Variables and Probability Density Function
stem: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{4}\) for an interval \(0 < x < c\). What is the value of the constant \(c\) that makes \(f(x)\) a valid probability density function?
solution:
Note that the integral of the p. d. f. over the support of the random variable must be
That is, \(\int_{0}^{c} f(x)\, dx = 1\).
That is, \(\int_{0}^{c}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{4}\right) dx = 1\). But, \(\int_{0}^{c}\left(\dfrac{x^3}{4}\right) dx = \left[\dfrac{x^4}{16}\right]_{0}^{c} = \dfrac{c^4}{16}\). Since this integral must be equal to 1,
we have \(\dfrac{c^4}{16} = 1\), or equivalently \(c^4 = 16\), so that \(c = 2\) since c must be positive.

Let's return to the example in which \(X\) has the following probability density function :
\(f(x) = 3x^2\)
for \(0 < x < 1\). What is the cumulative distribution function \(F(x)\)?

Let's return to the example in which \(X\) has the following probability density function :
\(f(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{4}\) for \(0 < x < 4\). What is the cumulative distribution function \(X\)?

Suppose the p.d.f. of a continuous random variable \(X\) is defined as:
\(f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 1, & \text{for } -1 < x < 0 \\ 1 - x, & \text{for } 0 \leq x < 1 \end{cases}\)
Find the c.d.f. \(F(x)\).
solution:
If we look the p.d.f. it is defined in two steps.
[Fig. 7.1 shows the graph of \(f(t)\): the triangle with vertices \((-1,\, 0)\), \((0,\, 1)\) and \((1,\, 0)\), with the region up to \(t = x\) shaded.]
Now for the other two intervals :
For \(-1 < x < 0\) and \(0 < x < 1\).
\(F(x) = \int_{-1}^{x}(x + 1)\, dx\)
\(= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} + x\right]_{-1}^{x} = \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2} + x\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - 1\right)\)
\(= \dfrac{x^2}{2} + x + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{x^2 + 2x + 2}{2}\)
\(= \dfrac{(x + 1)^2}{2}\)
\(F(0) = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
For \(0 < x < 1\)
\(F(x) = P(-1 < x < 1) = P(-1 < x < 0) + P(0 < x < 1) = \int_{-1}^{0}(x + 1)\, dx + \int_{0}^{x}(1 - x)\, dx\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2} + \int_{0}^{x}(1 - x)\, dx\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{2} + x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\)
\(F(x) = 0\), for \(x \leq -1\)
\(F(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}(x + 1)^2\), for \(-1 < x \leq 0\)
\(\quad\ \ = \dfrac{1}{2} + x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\), for \(0 < x < 1\)
\(\quad\ \ = 1\), for \(x \geq 1\)

subtopic: Continuous Random Variables and Probability Density Function
stem:
Verify if the following functions are p.d.f. of a continuous r.v. \(X\).
(i) \(f(x) = e^{-x}\), for \(0 < x < \infty\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.
(ii) \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2}\), for \(-2 < x < 2\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.
solution:
(i) \(e^{-x}\) is \(\geq 0\) for any value of \(x\) since \(e > 0\),
\(\therefore\ e^{-x} > 0\), for \(0 < x < \infty\)
\(\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x)\, dx = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x}\, dx = \left[-e^{-x}\right]_{0}^{\infty} = \left[\dfrac{1}{e^{\infty}} - e^{0}\right] = -(0 - 1) = 1\)
Both the conditions of p.d.f. are satisfied \(f(x)\) is p.d.f. of r.v.
(ii) \(f(x) < 0\) i.e. negative for \(-2 < x < 0\) therefore \(f(x)\) is not p.d.f.

subtopic: Continuous Random Variables and Probability Density Function
stem:
Find \(k\) if the following function is the p.d.f. of r.v. \(X\).
\(f(x) = kx^2(1 - x)\), for \(0 < x < 1\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.
solution:
Since \(f(x)\) is the p.d.f. of r.v. \(X\)
\(\int_{0}^{1} kx^2(1 - x)\, dx = 1\)
\(\therefore\ \int_{0}^{1} k(x^2 - x^3)\, dx = 1\)
\(\therefore\ k\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = 1\)
\(\therefore\ k\left\{\left[\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] - (0)\right\} = 1\)
\(\therefore\ k \times \dfrac{1}{12} = 1\)
\(\therefore\ k = 12\)

subtopic: Continuous Random Variables and Probability Density Function
stem:
For each of the following p.d.f. of r.v. \(X\), find (a) \(P(X < 1)\) and (b) \(P(|X| < 1)\)
(i) \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{18}\), for \(-3 < x < 3\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.
(ii) \(f(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{18}\), for \(-2 < x < 4\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.

Find the c.d.f. \(F(x)\) associated with p.d.f. \(f(x)\) of r.v. \(X\) where
\(f(x) = 3(1 - 2x^2)\), for \(0 < x < 1\) and \(= 0\), otherwise.
solution:
Since \(f(x)\) is p.d.f. of r.v. therefore c.d.f. is
\(F(x) = \int_{0}^{x} 3(1 - 2x^2)\, dx = \left[3\left(x - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right)\right]_{0}^{x} = \left[3x - 2x^3\right] = 3x - 2x^3\)
